                     stringsAsFactors = F)

1 Introduction

1.1 Overview

The Inc. 5000 is Inc. Magazine’s annual ranking of the fastest-growing private companies in the U.S. The list tracks companies based on their percentage revenue growth over a four-year period, offering a snapshot of how and where high-growth businesses are scaling. While headlines often focus on who made the top 10, there’s a much deeper story within the data — one that reveals how industry, geography, and company structure shape success.

This project explores what that story looks like. By analyzing company data from the 2014 Inc. 5000 list, the goal is to better understand the relationship between key variables like growth rate, revenue, industry, location, and company size, on the list. Specifically, the project looks at how different sectors and regions stack up in terms of growth, whether smaller companies are growing faster, and how company revenue relates to placement on the list.

Using a combination of R Graphs and Tableau, this analysis pairs statistical summaries and visualizations to surface trends that might not be obvious at first glance. The final product is an interactive Tableau Story with eight distinct story points, each focused on uncovering a different dimension of business growth and performance.

1.2 Methodology

The dataset used in this project comes from the 2014 Inc. 5000 Company List, which includes 5,000 companies with attributes such as:

rank: the company’s position on the Inc. 5000 list

growth: four-year percentage revenue growth

revenue: latest reported annual revenue

workers: number of employees

industry: company sector/category

state, city, metro: geographic info

yrs_on_list: how many times the company has appeared on the list

For this project, the main variables of interest are growth and revenue. These are analyzed alongside industry, geography (state and metro), employee size, and repeat appearances (yrs_on_list). Together, these variables help build a fuller picture of what drives business success at scale.

All data cleaning and preprocessing was done in R, including renaming variables, handling missing values, and dropping any unnecessary columns. Several plots including average revenue by industry, growth distributions, and revenue-to-growth comparisons were also created in R using ggplot2. These visualizations were then exported and imported into Tableau as part of a larger interactive project.

Each Tableau story point explores a different angle: which industries are most common, which grow the fastest, how geography plays a role, how revenue and employee size correlate with growth, and other key analysis. The aim is to present to those looking to start companies what it takes to grow a business in a robust economy.

2.2 Data Inspection

# Using the below loop to find any missing values.

cols <- colnames(Inc.df)

# missing values in each column: iterate
for (c in cols) {
  missing.rows <- which(is.na(Inc.df[,c]))
  
  num.missing <- length(missing.rows)
  
  s <- "no"
  
  if (num.missing > 0)
    s <- num.missing
  
  print(paste0("Column '", c, "' has ", 
                 s, " missing values"))}

3 R-Graphs and Analysis

3.1 Color Print-out

# I asked ChatGPT to give me some color recommendations since Inc. Magazine's colors are really just black and white. It printed the below for me. Hoping to use these colors throughout my presentation

corp_colors <- c("navy"    = "#1B365D",
  "teal"    = "#00A6A6",
  "green"   = "#2E8B57",
  "gold"    = "#FFD700",
  "charcoal"= "#4B4B4B")

3.2 Average Revenue v. Industry Chart

industry_avg_revenue <- Inc.df %>%
  group_by(industry) %>%
  summarise(avg_revenue = mean(revenue, na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
  arrange(desc(avg_revenue))

industry_avg_revenue <- industry_avg_revenue %>%
  mutate(industry = factor(industry, levels = rev(industry)))

ind_avg_plot <- ggplot(industry_avg_revenue, aes(x = avg_revenue, y = industry, fill = avg_revenue)) +
  geom_col(show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "#a8e6cf", high = "#379683") +  # light to deep green
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::dollar_format(scale = 1e-6, suffix = "M")) +
  labs(
    title = "Average Revenue by Industry",
    x = "Average Revenue ($)",
    y = "Industry"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_family = "Helvetica") +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 16),
    axis.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 12),
    axis.text = element_text(color = "black"),
    panel.grid.major.y = element_blank()
  )

ind_avg_plot

3.3 Growth v. Revenue Scatterplot

df_filtered_scatter <- Inc.df %>%
  filter(growth <= 10000, revenue <= 1e9)

growth.v.rev.plot <- ggplot(df_filtered_scatter, aes(x = revenue, y = growth)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5, color = "#379683") +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, color = "darkgray", linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::dollar_format(scale = 1e-6, suffix = "M")) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent_format(scale = 1)) +
  labs(
    title = "Growth vs. Revenue: Is There a Tradeoff?",
    x = "Revenue ($, Millions)",
    y = "4-Year Growth (%)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_family = "Helvetica") +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 16),
    axis.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 12),
    axis.text = element_text(color = "black"))

growth.v.rev.plot
## `geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x'

# Find the outliers (important for Tableau)
Inc.df.outliers <- Inc.df %>%
  mutate(growth_z = scale(growth))

# Filter for companies with growth z-score > 3 (very high growth)
outliers_z <- Inc.df.outliers %>%
  filter(growth_z > 3) %>%
  arrange(desc(growth))
## Warning: Using one column matrices in `filter()` was deprecated in dplyr 1.1.0.

Inc.df.revout <- Inc.df %>%
  mutate(revenue_z = scale(revenue))

outliers_revenue <- Inc.df.revout %>%
  filter(revenue_z > 3) %>%
  arrange(desc(revenue))

# View the top 10 companies with extreme revenue
head(outliers_revenue, 10)

3.4 Growth by Employee Size

employee_size <- Inc.df %>%
  mutate(size_group = case_when(
    workers <= 50 ~ "Small (1–50)",
    workers <= 200 ~ "Mid (51–200)",
    workers > 200 ~ "Large (200+)"))

df_filtered <- employee_size %>% filter(growth <= 10000)

employee_size_plot <- ggplot(df_filtered, aes(x = size_group, y = growth, fill = size_group)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.alpha = 0.3, show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent_format(scale = 1)) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(
    "Small (1–50)" = "#A8E6CF",
    "Mid (51–200)" = "#56C596",
    "Large (200+)" = "#379683"
  )) +
  labs(
    title = "Do Smaller Companies Grow Faster?",
    x = "Company Size Group (Employees)",
    y = "4-Year Growth (%)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_family = "Helvetica") +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 16),
    axis.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 12),
    axis.text = element_text(color = "black"))

employee_size_plot

# Will need it for Tableau
write.csv(employee_size, "employee_size_output.csv", row.names = FALSE)

3.5 Number of Years on List vs. Growth

df_filtered_years <- Inc.df %>% filter(growth <= 10000)

df_filtered_years <- df_filtered_years %>%
  mutate(yrs_on_list = factor(yrs_on_list, levels = sort(unique(yrs_on_list))))

# Create the boxplot
growth_by_years <- ggplot(df_filtered_years, aes(x = yrs_on_list, y = growth, fill = yrs_on_list)) +
  geom_boxplot(show.legend = FALSE, outlier.alpha = 0.2) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent_format(scale = 1)) +
  labs(
    title = "Do Repeat Companies Perform Differently?",
    subtitle = "4-Year Growth by Number of Times on the Inc. 5000 List",
    x = "Years on List",
    y = "4-Year Growth (%)"
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = rep("#379683", length(unique(df_filtered_years$yrs_on_list)))) +
  theme_minimal(base_family = "Helvetica") +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 16),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 12),
    axis.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 12),
    axis.text = element_text(color = "black"))

growth_by_years
